title: Unique Paths
summary: A robot moves only right or down on an m×n grid. Return the number of distinct paths from the top-left to the bottom-right corner.
statement:
A robot stands in the top-left corner of an `m × n` grid and wants to reach the bottom-right corner. It can only move right or down, one cell at a time.

Return the number of distinct paths. The answer is at most `2 × 10^9`.
hints: The only ways into a cell are from the cell above it and from the cell to its left.
paths[r][c] = paths[r − 1][c] + paths[r][c − 1], with every cell of the first row and column equal to 1.
One row of the table is enough. It is also a combination: C(m + n − 2, m − 1).
explain: Every path from the top-left to the bottom-right of a 3 × 7 grid makes 2 moves down and 6 moves right, 8 moves in all. Choosing which 2 of the 8 are "down" gives C(8, 2) = 28 paths.

title: Unique Paths II
summary: Like Unique Paths, but cells marked 1 are obstacles. Return the number of paths moving only right or down.
statement:
As in "Unique Paths", a robot moves only right or down from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell. Now `obstacleGrid[i][j]` is `1` for an obstacle and `0` for a free cell, and the robot cannot enter obstacles.

Return the number of distinct paths. If the start or end is blocked, the answer is `0`.
hints: Use the same recurrence as "Unique Paths", but a cell with an obstacle has 0 paths.
Careful with the first row and column: past an obstacle, nothing further along can be reached.
A single array works: set dp[c] = 0 on an obstacle, otherwise dp[c] += dp[c − 1].
explain: The obstacle in the centre blocks every path through the middle. That leaves two routes: right, right, down, down along the top edge, and down, down, right, right along the left edge. So the answer is 2.

title: Minimum Path Sum
summary: Moving only right or down, return the smallest possible sum of a path from the top-left to the bottom-right cell.
statement:
`grid` contains non-negative numbers. Find a path from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down, that has the smallest possible sum of the numbers along it.

Return that sum.
hints: The cheapest way into a cell comes from the cheaper of the cell above and the cell to the left.
cost[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(cost[r − 1][c], cost[r][c − 1]); the first row and column only have one way in.
You can update the grid in place or keep a single row.
explain: The path 1 → 3 → 1 → 1 → 1 (right, right, down, down) adds up to 7, and no other path of right and down moves is cheaper. So the answer is 7.

title: Triangle
summary: From the top of the triangle, move to an adjacent number on the row below each step. Return the minimum path sum to the bottom.

perf.label: 200 rows
perf.gen: List<List<Integer>> a0 = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) a0.add(BCB.list(BCB.ints(i + 1, -10000, 10000)));

statement:
`triangle` has one value in its first row, two in its second, and so on. Starting at the top, each step moves to an adjacent value in the row below: from index `i` you can go to index `i` or `i + 1`.

Return the minimum sum of a path from the top to the bottom row.
hints: Going top-down, each cell has two parents and the edges need special cases. Try going bottom-up.
Start with the bottom row. Each cell above becomes its value plus the smaller of its two children.
After processing all rows, the top holds the answer. One array the size of the bottom row is enough.
explain: Going down 2 → 3 → 5 → 1, each step to an adjacent number in the row below, adds up to 11, the smallest possible. So the answer is 11.

title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
summary: A falling path starts in the first row and moves to the cell below, below-left or below-right each step. Return the minimum sum of any falling path.
statement:
`matrix` is `n × n`. A falling path starts at any cell of the first row and, at each step, moves to the next row: directly below, below-left or below-right.

Return the minimum sum of any falling path.
hints: The best path to a cell comes from one of the three cells above it.
best[r][c] = matrix[r][c] + min(best[r − 1][c − 1], best[r − 1][c], best[r − 1][c + 1]), skipping columns that are out of range.
The answer is the minimum of the last row. Keeping only the previous row gives O(n) space.
explain: Start at 1 in the top row, fall to 5 (straight down) and then to 7 (down-left): 1 + 5 + 7 = 13. The path 1 → 4 → 8 also sums to 13, and nothing is smaller, so the answer is 13.

title: Maximal Square
summary: In a grid of "0"/"1" characters, return the area of the largest square containing only "1"s.
statement:
`matrix` is filled with the characters `'0'` and `'1'`. Return the area of the largest square that contains only `'1'`s.

The square must be axis-aligned and every cell inside it must be `'1'`. Return its area, the side length squared, or 0 if the matrix has no `'1'` at all.
hints: Let side[r][c] be the side of the largest all-1 square whose bottom-right corner is (r, c).
If the cell is "1", side[r][c] = 1 + min(side above, side to the left, side above-left). Any of the three can limit the square.
Track the largest side and return its square. One row of the table plus a variable for the diagonal is enough.
explain: The largest all-`1` square is 2 × 2, for example rows 1–2 and columns 2–3 (counting from 0). No 3 × 3 block is all ones, so the answer is its area, 4.

title: Count Square Submatrices with All Ones
summary: Count every square submatrix (of any size) made entirely of 1s.

perf.label: a 300×300 matrix
perf.gen: int[][] a0 = new int[300][300]; for (int[] row : a0) for (int j = 0; j < 300; j++) row[j] = BCB.R.nextInt(10) == 0 ? 0 : 1;

statement:
`matrix` contains `0`s and `1`s. Count every square submatrix, of any size, that is made entirely of `1`s.

A 2 × 2 block of ones contains five such squares: four of size 1 and one of size 2.

Squares of different sizes and positions are all counted, even when they overlap. A useful fact: the number of squares whose bottom-right corner is a given cell equals the side of the largest one there.
hints: Use the same table as "Maximal Square": side[r][c] = the largest all-ones square ending at (r, c).
A square of side k ending at (r, c) also contains squares of sides k − 1, …, 1 ending there, so the cell contributes side[r][c] squares.
Sum side[r][c] over all cells.
explain: There are 10 cells containing 1 (squares of side 1), 4 all-ones squares of side 2 and 1 of side 3. In total 10 + 4 + 1 = 15.

title: Dungeon Game
summary: A knight walks right or down from the top-left to the bottom-right room; each room adds or removes health, and health must stay above 0. Return the minimum starting health.
statement:
A knight starts in the top-left room of `dungeon` and must reach the princess in the bottom-right room, moving only right or down. Each room changes his health by `dungeon[i][j]` (negative values hurt, positive values heal). If his health ever drops to 0 or below, he dies.

Return the minimum health he needs at the start.
hints: Working forward is hard because you have to balance the health needed now against the health gained later.
Work backward from the princess: need[r][c] is the health needed when entering room (r, c).
need[r][c] = max(1, min(need[r + 1][c], need[r][c + 1]) − dungeon[r][c]), with the last room needing max(1, 1 − its value).
explain: The best route is right, right, down, down through -2, -3, 3, 1 and -5. Starting with 7 health, the knight never drops below 1 (7 → 5 → 2 → 5 → 6 → 1), and starting with 6 he would. So the answer is 7.

title: Cherry Pickup
summary: Cells are 1 (cherry), 0 (empty) or −1 (thorn). Walk from the top-left to the bottom-right moving right/down, then back moving left/up, collecting cherries (each picked once). Return the most cherries, or 0 if no valid trip exists.
statement:
`grid` is `n × n`. Each cell is `1` (a cherry), `0` (empty) or `-1` (a thorn you cannot pass). Walk from the top-left to the bottom-right moving only right or down, then walk back to the top-left moving only left or up, picking up every cherry you pass (a cell's cherry can be picked only once).

Return the maximum number of cherries you can collect, or `0` if there is no valid trip.
constraints: The start and end cells are not thorns
hints: Doing the best trip there and then the best trip back is not optimal. Treat it as two people walking from the start at the same time.
After t steps both people are on the diagonal r + c = t, so the state (t, r1, r2) determines both positions.
For each state, take the best of the four combinations of previous moves, and add the cherries at both cells (only once if they are on the same cell). Thorns make a state invalid.
explain: Going down, down, right, right picks the cherries at (1,0), (2,0), (2,1) and (2,2): 4 cherries. Coming back up the other side picks the remaining one at (0,1). That makes 5, the most possible.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
summary: Moving up, down, left or right, return the length of the longest path whose values strictly increase at every step.
statement: Return the length of the longest **strictly increasing** path in `matrix`. From each cell you can move left, right, up or down (not diagonally, and not outside the matrix), and each step must go to a strictly larger value.
hints: Let f(r, c) be the longest increasing path starting at (r, c). It is 1 plus the best f over neighbours with a larger value.
Increasing paths can never loop back, so f has no cycles and can be memoised: each cell is computed once.
Without recursion: count each cell's larger neighbours, peel off the cells with none (local maxima) layer by layer like Kahn's algorithm; the number of layers is the answer.
explain: One longest path is 1 → 2 → 6 → 9: from the 1 in the bottom row, up to 2, up to 6, up to 9. No path is longer, so the answer is 4.
